microtopics.title: Oxidation number, oxidation/reduction and agents
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must coordinate formal oxidation-state bookkeeping with electron transfer and avoid the common agent-name inversion.
entry_assumptions: Can read chemical equations, ionic charges and integer oxidation-state labels when the bookkeeping rules are supplied.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Oxidation number is a formal assignment whose increase corresponds to oxidation and decrease to reduction; an oxidising agent is itself reduced while a reducing agent is itself oxidised.

teaching_path.action: Apply oxidation-number priority rules and require the algebraic sum to equal the species charge.
teaching_path.why_valid: The assignment is a formal bookkeeping convention constrained by overall charge.
teaching_path.output: Charge reconciliation closes the oxidation-number ledger.

teaching_path.action: Track the same element from reactant to product and classify increases as oxidation and decreases as reduction.
teaching_path.why_valid: A direction can only be named after matching the element across both sides.
teaching_path.output: Electron-loss/gain and oxidation-number change are two views of the same bookkeeping.

teaching_path.action: Name the species being reduced as the oxidising agent and the species being oxidised as the reducing agent.
teaching_path.why_valid: Agent names describe the process caused in the partner, not the self-change.
teaching_path.output: Separating self-change from agent role prevents reversal.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Oxidation number is a literal measured atomic charge, and the species oxidised is the oxidising agent.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can resonance/electron sharing make physical charge differ from formal oxidation number, and what happens to the electron acceptor itself?
misconceptions.repair: Label oxidation state as formal bookkeeping; write self-change first, then assign the opposite process as the agent name.

exit_task.prompt: Why is an oxidation number useful even though it is not generally a measured atomic charge?

answer.summary: Its formal assignment rules consistently expose electron-accounting changes between reactants and products.
reasoning: The convention assigns electrons by defined rules.
Changes in the assignments reveal coupled oxidation and reduction.
answer.check: Use the phrase formal assignment and verify the total-charge sum.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: Qualitative bookkeeping explanation; no new computed numerical oracle is asserted.

microtopics.research_contribution: Carries the corrected oxidation-state, agent, classification, balancing and n-factor boundaries from the PR #376 audit into governed records; independent exact-render review remains pending.

construction_units.decision: Oxidation number is a formal assignment whose increase corresponds to oxidation and decrease to reduction; an oxidising agent is itself reduced while a reducing agent is itself oxidised.

independent_checks.statement: Use the phrase formal assignment and verify the total-charge sum.

microtopics.title: Redox classification, displacement and disproportionation patterns
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must distinguish chemical change from redox and identify split/convergent oxidation-state patterns.
entry_assumptions: Can read chemical equations, ionic charges and integer oxidation-state labels when the bookkeeping rules are supplied.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A reaction is redox only when oxidation-number bookkeeping shows coupled increase and decrease; reaction labels such as decomposition or displacement do not replace that test.

teaching_path.action: Recognise the chemical reaction without yet calling it redox.
teaching_path.why_valid: Formation of new substances is not sufficient evidence of electron-transfer bookkeeping.
teaching_path.output: Chemical-change classification and redox classification are separate questions.

teaching_path.action: Compare oxidation numbers on both sides and require at least one increase coupled to a decrease.
teaching_path.why_valid: A double displacement can be non-redox, while a displacement can be redox depending on actual state changes.
teaching_path.output: Oxidation-state change is the deciding test.

teaching_path.action: For the same element, map one initial state splitting upward and downward as disproportionation, and two starting states converging as comproportionation.
teaching_path.why_valid: The classification depends on the directed oxidation-state map.
teaching_path.output: Counting how many states appear is not enough.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every chemical reaction is redox, and any reaction showing three oxidation states is disproportionation.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can ions exchange partners with unchanged oxidation numbers, and are the three states arranged as one-to-two or two-to-one across the reaction arrow?
misconceptions.repair: Run the oxidation-number change check first, then draw the directed state map before naming a special redox pattern.

exit_task.prompt: Why is decomposition alone insufficient to call a reaction redox?

answer.summary: Decomposition describes a reaction pattern, whereas redox requires actual oxidation-number changes.
reasoning: A decomposition can occur without changing oxidation states.
The redox test is independent electron/oxidation-state bookkeeping.
answer.check: List oxidation states before and after rather than relying on the reaction-type label.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: Qualitative bookkeeping explanation; no new computed numerical oracle is asserted.

construction_units.decision: A reaction is redox only when oxidation-number bookkeeping shows coupled increase and decrease; reaction labels such as decomposition or displacement do not replace that test.

microtopics.title: Half-reaction balancing and reaction-dependent n-factor
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must conserve atoms and charge in a declared medium and derive electron-change counts from the specified reaction rather than memorising them as universal properties.
entry_assumptions: Can read chemical equations, ionic charges and integer oxidation-state labels when the bookkeeping rules are supplied.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Half-reaction balancing is a conservation algorithm, while n-factor compresses the electron change for one specified redox transformation; neither is valid without the reaction context.

teaching_path.action: State acidic or basic aqueous medium before choosing balancing species.
teaching_path.why_valid: The allowed bookkeeping species depend on the declared medium.
teaching_path.output: Medium is part of the problem conditions.

teaching_path.action: Balance atoms and charge within each half-reaction, then scale so electrons cancel when the halves are added.
teaching_path.why_valid: Electrons are transfer bookkeeping and must not remain in the final net reaction.
teaching_path.output: The final equation must conserve every element and total charge.

teaching_path.action: Derive n-factor from the electron change and stoichiometric role in the specified balanced reaction.
teaching_path.why_valid: The same substance can participate in different redox changes and therefore have different reaction-specific n-factors.
teaching_path.output: Equivalent-mass use is tied to that reaction context.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Matching atom counts is enough even if charge differs, and every reagent has one universal n-factor.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Would an ionic equation with equal atom counts but unequal total charge be balanced, and can the same reagent form products at different oxidation states?
misconceptions.repair: Keep separate atom and charge ledgers, and derive n-factor from the actual balanced transformation each time.

exit_task.prompt: Why can a redox reagent have different n-factors in different reactions?

answer.summary: Because n-factor is the reaction-specific number of electrons transferred per formula amount, and that electron change can differ with the product and oxidation-state pathway.
reasoning: Molar mass is tied to the formula.
n-factor is tied to the specified electron-transfer role.
answer.check: Write the reaction or oxidation-state change beside every n-factor value.

questions.stem: Species A gains electrons from species B. Which species is the oxidising agent and why?
conditions: Use the formal redox bookkeeping model and reaction conditions stated in the surrounding Core1A construction.

answer.summary: Species A is the oxidising agent because A is reduced while causing B to be oxidised.
reasoning: A gains electrons, so A undergoes reduction.
The electrons come from B, so B is oxidised.
The species causing oxidation of its partner is the oxidising agent.
answer.check: The oxidising agent must appear on the reduction side of the bookkeeping.

difficulty.basis: Single-concept authored worked anchor after instruction.

questions.stem: The same element begins in one oxidation state and appears in two products, one at a higher and one at a lower oxidation state. What pattern is this?
conditions: Use the formal redox bookkeeping model and reaction conditions stated in the surrounding Core1A construction.

reasoning: One starting oxidation state is both oxidised and reduced in different product portions.
The state map branches upward and downward from the same initial value.
answer.check: Both an increase and a decrease must originate from the same initial oxidation state.

difficulty.basis: Single-concept authored worked anchor after instruction.

questions.stem: What two independent conservation checks close a balanced ionic redox equation?
conditions: Use the formal redox bookkeeping model and reaction conditions stated in the surrounding Core1A construction.

answer.summary: Every element count and the total electric charge must match on both sides.
reasoning: Ionic redox equations also conserve total charge.
Half-reaction electrons must cancel from the net equation.
answer.check: Make an element-count table and a separate algebraic charge sum.
